source_text: Ideo et cum orandi legem daret, addidit dicens: et cum steteritis ad orationem, remittite si quid habetis aduersus aliquem, ut et pater uester qui in caelis est remittat peccata uobis. et ad sacrificium cum dissensione uenientem reuocat ab altari et iubet prius concordare cum fratre, tunc cum pace redeuntem Deo munus offerre, quia nec ad Cain munera respexit Deus: neque enim habere pacatum Deum poterat qui cum fratre pacem per zeli discordiam non habebat. quam sibi igitur pacem promittunt inimici fratrum? quae sacrificia celebrare se credunt aemuli sacerdotum? secum esse Christum, cum collecti fuerint, opinantur qui extra Christi ecclesiam colliguntur?
thought_title: Prayer, sacrifice, and peace with a brother
orientation: Cyprian is arguing that those who break the Church's unity cannot have peace with God, and he now applies this to prayer and sacrifice.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore also when he gave the law of praying, he added saying: and when you stand for prayer, forgive if you have anything against anyone, so that also your Father who is in heaven may forgive sins to you. And one coming to sacrifice with dissension he calls back from the altar and orders first to be reconciled with a brother, then returning with peace to offer a gift to God, because God did not even look upon the gifts of Cain: for he could not have God at peace who did not have peace with a brother through the discord of envy. What peace therefore do enemies of brothers promise themselves? What sacrifices do rivals of priests believe they celebrate? Do they think that Christ is with them, when they have been gathered, who are gathered outside the Church of Christ?

choices.english: to be reconciled with a brother
choices.why: The verb concordare here means to restore harmony, not merely to agree; 'be reconciled' captures the required restoration of peace before sacrifice.
rejected: to make concord with a brother

choices.why: Aemuli here denotes those who set themselves up in opposition to the legitimate priests; 'rivals' keeps the hostile, competitive force.

choices.english: are gathered outside the Church of Christ
choices.why: The passive colliguntur is deliberate: they may assemble, but their gathering is outside the one Church; 'are gathered' preserves the passive and the spatial exclusion.
rejected: gather themselves outside the Church of Christ
assemble outside the Church of Christ

choices.why: Zelus here is the envious rivalry that destroys brotherly peace; 'envy' is the concrete vice, and 'discord' keeps the abstract result.

pass_b_english: So when he gave the rule for praying, he added these words: “And when you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father in heaven may forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25). And he calls back from the altar the one who comes to sacrifice while at odds with a brother, and orders him first to be reconciled with his brother, and then to return in peace and offer his gift to God (Matthew 5:23-24). For God did not even look upon Cain’s gifts (Genesis 4:5), since no one who lacked peace with his brother through the discord of envy could have God at peace with him. What peace, then, do the enemies of brothers promise themselves? What sacrifices do rivals of priests believe they are celebrating? Do those who are gathered outside the Church of Christ imagine that Christ is with them when they assemble?

last_rejected.source_quote: et cum steteritis ad orationem, remittite si quid habetis aduersus aliquem, ut et pater uester qui in caelis est remittat peccata uobis
last_rejected.why: The quotation matches Mark 11:25 in modern Bibles, but Cyprian's source text follows the Old Latin which here reflects Matthew 6:14-15 / Mark 11:25 blending; however, the parallel passage in Matthew 5:23-24 is cited next. The issue: Cyprian's source for the first quote is likely Matthew 6:14-15 (remittite...remittat), not Mark 11:25. The English Mark 11:25 is a modern harmonization that misattributes Cyprian's source.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'cum steteritis ad orationem' matches Mark 11:25; adding a scripture reference is standard scholarly aid, not a translation error.

last_rejected.quote: So when he gave the rule for praying, he added these words
last_rejected.source_quote: Ideo et cum orandi legem daret, addidit dicens
last_rejected.why: The English 'he' obscures that Christ is the speaker giving this rule; Cyprian presents this as the Lord's teaching, continuing from previous sections where Christ speaks to Peter and the disciples.
last_rejected.fix: So when the Lord gave the rule for praying, he added these words
last_rejected.ruling: 'He' is a normal pronoun for 'daret'; antecedent is clear from context. Not a meaning change or reader misleading.
